statement: Thermally dimorphic fungi, such as Coccidioides, undergo a physiological transition loop regulated by the ambient temperature. Which of the following accurately describes this structural transition?
options: They form nonseptate hyphae in the environment and septate hyphae in the host
The transition is triggered by the high osmotic pressure of human blood
The fungi lose their chitin cell wall upon entering the human body to avoid immune detection
They exist as yeasts in the soil at 25°C and as molds in human tissue at 37°C
They exist as molds in the soil at 25°C and as yeasts or spherules in tissue at 37°C
correctOption: They exist as molds in the soil at 25°C and as yeasts or spherules in tissue at 37°C
optionExplanations: Dimorphism refers to the yeast/mold transition, not a change in the presence of septa within the hyphae themselves.
While many factors exist, temperature is the primary physiological trigger for 'thermal' dimorphism.
Fungi do not lose their cell wall in the host; the cell wall (chitin/glucan) is essential for their structural integrity at all stages.
This is the reverse of the actual transition; fungi are molds in the colder environment and yeasts in the warmer host.

Thermal dimorphism is a regulatory loop where the fungus senses temperature. At room temperature (ambient), they grow as molds (hyphae). Upon inhalation and exposure to 37°C (body temperature), they shift their gene expression to form yeasts or spherules.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 399 (Book Page): Several medically important fungi are thermally dimorphic... They exist as molds in the environment at ambient temperature and as yeasts (or other structures such as the spherules of Coccidioides) in human tissues at body temperature.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: Tinea versicolor, caused by Malassezia species, is most commonly identified clinically by which of the following skin changes?
options: Hypopigmented areas on tanned skin
Brownish-black spots on the palms of the hands
Wartlike lesions with crusting abscesses
Honey-colored crusts on the perioral region
Pruritic vesicles arranged in a circular 'ring' border
correctOption: Hypopigmented areas on tanned skin
optionExplanations: Malassezia interferes with melanin production. In summer, the surrounding normal skin tans while the infected areas do not, making the hypopigmented plaques obvious.
Brownish spots on the palms are characteristic of tinea nigra, caused by Cladosporium werneckii.
Wartlike lesions with abscesses along lymphatics describe chromomycosis, caused by various dematiaceous soil fungi.
Honey-colored crusts are the classic description of impetigo, a bacterial infection usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes.
Circular inflammatory rings with central clearing describe ringworm (tinea corporis), caused by dermatophytes.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 409 (Book Page): The lesions are usually noticed as hypopigmented areas, especially on tanned skin in the summer... it is caused by Malassezia species.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: Which of the following fungal groups is characterized by its ability to infect only superficial keratinized structures such as the skin, hair, and nails, without invading deeper tissues?
options: Dematiaceous fungi
Dermatophytes
Dimorphic systemic fungi
Subcutaneous molds
Opportunistic yeasts
correctOption: Dermatophytes
optionExplanations: Dematiaceous fungi are dark-colored fungi that cause chromomycosis, a deep granulomatous infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue, rather than being limited to keratinized structures.

Dermatophytes (Trichophyton, Microsporum, and Epidermophyton) are specialized molds that utilize keratin as a nutrient source, limiting their pathology to the non-living keratinized layers of the epithelium.
Systemic fungi such as Histoplasma and Coccidioides are dimorphic but primarily infect internal organs after inhalation, rather than being restricted to keratinized layers.
Subcutaneous molds, such as Sporothrix, typically enter via trauma and involve the dermis and lymphatic vessels, moving beyond the superficial keratinized layers.
Opportunistic yeasts like Candida can cause superficial infections (thrush) but are also capable of deep tissue invasion and hematogenous dissemination in compromised hosts.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 407 (Book Page): Dermatophytoses are caused by fungi (dermatophytes) that infect only superficial keratinized structures (skin, hair, and nails), not deeper tissues.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: Which statement best characterizes the thermal dimorphism exhibited by Histoplasma capsulatum?
options: It is not dimorphic and exists only as a single-celled budding yeast
It exists as a mold at both 25°C and 37°C, but changes spore types
It exists as a yeast at room temperature and as a spherule at body temperature
It exists as a yeast in the soil and as a mold in human tissue
It exists as a mold in the environment and a yeast in human tissue
correctOption: It exists as a mold in the environment and a yeast in human tissue
optionExplanations: Dermatophytes and Malassezia are not thermally dimorphic in the same way as the systemic fungi; Histoplasma is explicitly defined by its dimorphic nature in its life cycle.
Thermal dimorphism specifically refers to the change in vegetative growth form (mold vs yeast/spherule) based on temperature, not just a change in spore morphology within a mold phase.
The spherule form is unique to Coccidioides immitis, not Histoplasma capsulatum, and Histoplasma exists as a mold at room temperature, not a yeast.
This is the reverse of the actual transition; systemic dimorphic fungi like Histoplasma are molds in the colder environment and yeasts in the warmer host.
Histoplasma capsulatum is a classic dimorphic fungus. It grows as a mold (with macroconidia and microconidia) in the soil and converts to a yeast form in the host tissues (37°C).
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 414 (Book Page): H. capsulatum is a dimorphic fungus that exists as a mold in soil and as a yeast in tissue.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: When performing a direct microscopic examination of clinical specimens, how can the tissue phase of Sporothrix schenckii be most reliably distinguished from the tissue phase of Histoplasma capsulatum?
options: Round or cigar-shaped yeasts in Sporothrix vs. oval yeasts within macrophages in Histoplasma
Presence of endospores within spherules in Sporothrix vs. budding yeasts in Histoplasma
Presence of septate hyphae in Sporothrix vs. nonseptate hyphae in Histoplasma
Thick-walled yeasts with broad-based buds in Sporothrix vs. multiple buds in Histoplasma
Mixture of hyphae and yeasts in Sporothrix vs. only microconidia in Histoplasma
correctOption: Round or cigar-shaped yeasts in Sporothrix vs. oval yeasts within macrophages in Histoplasma
optionExplanations: Sporothrix is characterized by cigar-shaped yeasts in tissue, whereas Histoplasma is found as small oval yeasts sequestered within the cytoplasm of reticuloendothelial cells.
Spherules containing endospores are the pathognomonic tissue form of Coccidioides immitis, not Sporothrix or Histoplasma.
Both fungi are dimorphic and exist as yeasts in human tissue, not as hyphae; hyphae are typically found in the environment or laboratory culture at room temperature.
Broad-based buds are characteristic of Blastomyces, and multiple buds (ship's captain wheel) are characteristic of Paracoccidioides, not the organisms in question.
A mixture of hyphae and yeasts is the classic 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance of Malassezia furfur, while Histoplasma exists solely in the yeast form in human tissue specimens.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 409 (Book Page): KOH prep shows cigar-shaped yeasts [for Sporothrix]. Page 415 (Book Page): In tissue biopsy specimens or bone marrow aspirates, oval yeast cells within macrophages are seen [for Histoplasma].

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: Which of the following clinical diagnostic criteria is specifically used to rapidly screen for Tinea capitis caused by certain species of the genus Microsporum?
options: Growth of colonies on Sabouraud’s agar with low pH
Fluorescence under ultraviolet light from a Wood’s lamp
Presence of pseudohyphae in a KOH preparation
Positive delayed hypersensitivity skin test to Trichophytin
Detection of urea breath test positivity
correctOption: Fluorescence under ultraviolet light from a Wood’s lamp
optionExplanations: While Sabouraud's agar is used for growth, it is not a 'rapid screening' method for specific genera like the Wood's lamp.
Microsporum species possess metabolites that fluoresce under UV light (Wood's lamp), making it a specific and rapid diagnostic tool for tinea capitis.
Pseudohyphae are characteristic of Candida species, not dermatophytes like Microsporum.
Skin tests for dermatophytes exist but are not used as the standard rapid diagnostic criteria for scalp ringworm.
Urea breath tests are used for Helicobacter pylori bacteria, not for fungal skin infections.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 409 (Book Page): Tinea capitis lesions caused by Microsporum species can be detected by seeing fluorescence when the lesions are exposed to ultraviolet light from a Wood’s lamp.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: A 40-year-old landscaper presents with a painless ulcer on her right thumb and a series of subcutaneous nodules extending up her forearm. If the causative agent is Sporothrix schenckii, which morphological transition would be expected in the clinical laboratory?
options: Yeasts with broad-based buds at 25°C converting to molds at 37°C
Radiating chains of conidia at both 20°C and 37°C
Spherules at 25°C converting to septate hyphae at 37°C
Molds with daisy-like conidia at 20°C converting to cigar-shaped yeasts at 37°C
Nonseptate hyphae at all temperatures without yeast forms
correctOption: Molds with daisy-like conidia at 20°C converting to cigar-shaped yeasts at 37°C
optionExplanations: This describes the morphology of Blastomyces, but the temperatures for mold/yeast phases are reversed.
Radiating chains of conidia are characteristic of Aspergillus, which is a monomorphic mold, not a dimorphic fungus.
This describes Coccidioides, but reversed (mold in environment, spherule in tissue).
Sporothrix is dimorphic; the environmental mold (daisy-like) converts to the tissue yeast (cigar-shaped) at body temperature.
Sporothrix is dimorphic and has a yeast phase; nonseptate hyphae are characteristic of Zygomycetes like Mucor.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 409 (Book Page): Sporothrix schenckii is a dimorphic fungus. The mold form lives on plants, and the yeast form occurs in human tissue. ... In the clinical laboratory, round or cigar-shaped budding yeasts are seen in tissue specimens. In culture at room temperature, hyphae occurs bearing oval conidia in clusters at the tip of slender conidiophores (resembling a daisy).

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: Dermatophytes such as Trichophyton and Epidermophyton possess a specific tropism for which of the following tissues?
options: Subcutaneous adipose tissue
Skeletal muscle fibers
Central nervous system meninges
Vascular endothelial linings
Keratinized structures (skin, hair, nails)
correctOption: Keratinized structures (skin, hair, nails)
optionExplanations: Dermatophytes are superficial fungi and do not invade deeper tissues like subcutaneous fat or the subcutis.
Dermatophytes lack the enzymes to digest muscle tissue; they are specialized to utilize keratin as a nitrogen and energy source.
Meningeal infection is a characteristic of systemic or opportunistic fungi like Coccidioides or Cryptococcus, never dermatophytes.
Vascular invasion is a feature of opportunistic molds like Mucor or Aspergillus, but dermatophytes do not spread through or infect the vascular endothelium.
The defining characteristic of dermatophytes is their ability to digest and live on keratin, limiting their infection to the skin, hair, and nails.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 407 (Book Page): [Dermatophytoses are caused by fungi (dermatophytes) that infect only superficial keratinized structures (skin, hair, and nails), not deeper tissues.]

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: During a microscopic examination using a 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation of skin scrapings, how can a clinician distinguish Malassezia species from Trichophyton species?
options: Malassezia presents as a mixture of budding yeasts and hyphae, whereas Trichophyton presents only as septate hyphae.
Malassezia forms spherules containing endospores, whereas Trichophyton forms arthrospores.
Malassezia shows nonseptate hyphae, whereas Trichophyton shows septate hyphae.
Malassezia is found only within macrophages, whereas Trichophyton is extracellular.
Malassezia lacks a cell wall, whereas Trichophyton contains chitin.
correctOption: Malassezia presents as a mixture of budding yeasts and hyphae, whereas Trichophyton presents only as septate hyphae.
optionExplanations: The 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance (yeasts plus hyphae) is diagnostic for Malassezia, while dermatophytes like Trichophyton appear only as branching septate hyphae.
Spherules are characteristic of Coccidioides, not Malassezia; Trichophyton produces hyphae and conidia but is best known for septate hyphae in KOH.
Both Malassezia and dermatophytes like Trichophyton are characterized by the presence of hyphae, but their distinction lies in the additional presence of yeast cells in Malassezia.
Neither Malassezia nor Trichophyton are intracellular pathogens; Histoplasma is the fungus famously found inside macrophages.
All fungi, including Malassezia and Trichophyton, possess a cell wall containing chitin and glucans; they cannot be distinguished by its presence alone.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 409 (Book Page): The lesions [of Tinea Versicolor] contain both budding yeast cells and hyphae. Diagnosis is usually made by observing this mixture in KOH preparations... [Page 409 (Book Page) for Trichophyton]: KOH prep shows septate hyphae.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: Host defense against dermatophyte infections is mediated by several factors. Which physiological change or substance is specifically cited as an inhibitor of dermatophyte growth, explaining why tinea capitis is less common after puberty?
options: Alkaline secretions of the sweat glands
Fatty acids in the skin
Secretory IgA in the nasopharynx
Beta-glucan receptors on neutrophils
Low pH of the gastric mucosa
correctOption: Fatty acids in the skin
optionExplanations: Skin surfaces are generally acidic, and it is the presence of specific inhibitory fatty acids, rather than alkaline secretions, that provides the protection mentioned in the text.
The skin produces fatty acids that have antifungal properties. The increase in sebum and hormonal changes at puberty specifically help inhibit the growth of Trichophyton on the scalp.
Secretory IgA is vital for mucosal immunity in the respiratory and GI tracts but is not the primary factor limiting tinea capitis on the keratinized skin of the scalp.
Dectin (beta-glucan receptor) on innate immune cells is important for recognizing many fungi, but the specific age-related resistance to tinea capitis is attributed to skin fatty acids.
Gastric pH is a defense against ingested pathogens but does not influence fungal growth on the scalp or skin.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 400 (Book Page)-414: Fatty acids in the skin inhibit dermatophyte growth, and hormone-associated skin changes at puberty limit ringworm of the scalp caused by Trichophyton.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: Which genus of dermatophytes is characterized by its ability to be transmitted to humans from domestic animals such as dogs and cats, necessitating treatment of the animal to prevent reinfection?
options: Sporothrix
Microsporum
Trichophyton
Malassezia
Epidermophyton
correctOption: Microsporum
optionExplanations: Sporothrix is not a dermatophyte; it is a dimorphic fungus causing subcutaneous mycosis, typically introduced via trauma such as a rose thorn prick.
Microsporum is unique among the dermatophytes for its significant association with animal-to-human transmission, particularly from common household pets like cats and dogs.
Trichophyton species are primarily spread from person to person; while they cause various tinea infections, they are not the primary genus associated with transmission from household pets.
Malassezia species cause tinea versicolor and are part of the normal human skin flora; they are not classified as dermatophytes nor spread by domestic animals.
Epidermophyton is a genus of dermatophytes that infects the skin and nails but is typically transmitted among humans rather than being zoonotic from cats and dogs.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 407 (Book Page): Microsporum is also spread from animals such as dogs and cats. This indicates that to prevent reinfection by Microsporum, the animal must also be treated.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: Which finding in a 10% KOH preparation of skin scrapings is diagnostic for a superficial infection caused by Malassezia species?
options: A mixture of budding yeast cells and hyphae.
Nonseptate hyphae with black sporangiospores.
Dichotomously branching septate hyphae.
Arthrospores with alternating empty cells.
Spherules containing numerous endospores.
correctOption: A mixture of budding yeast cells and hyphae.
optionExplanations: Correct. Malassezia (the cause of Tinea versicolor) shows a classic 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance on KOH prep, consisting of short hyphae and budding yeasts.
Incorrect. This describes Mucor or Rhizopus, which are opportunistic molds.
Incorrect. This is more characteristic of Aspergillus species, which are opportunistic molds, not the cause of tinea versicolor.
Incorrect. Arthrospores with alternating empty cells are characteristic of Coccidioides immitis in soil/culture.
Incorrect. Spherules are the tissue form of Coccidioides, not Malassezia.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 409 (Book Page): The lesions contain both budding yeast cells and hyphae. Diagnosis is usually made by observing this mixture in KOH preparations.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of Coccidioides, Paracoccidioides, Blastomyces, Candida, Mucor, Aspergillus, and Cryptococcus
statement: When performing a microscopic examination of tissue specimens to differentiate systemic mycoses, how does the yeast form of Blastomyces dermatitidis contrast with Cryptococcus neoformans?
options: Blastomyces is found within macrophages, whereas Cryptococcus is strictly extracellular with septate hyphae.
Blastomyces forms a broad-based bud, whereas Cryptococcus forms a narrow-based bud.
Blastomyces forms multiple buds (ship captain's wheel), whereas Cryptococcus is a non-budding spherule.
Blastomyces has a wide polysaccharide capsule, whereas Cryptococcus has a doubly refractive wall with no capsule.
Blastomyces is a non-septate mold in tissue, whereas Cryptococcus is a dimorphic yeast.
correctOption: Blastomyces forms a broad-based bud, whereas Cryptococcus forms a narrow-based bud.
optionExplanations: Histoplasma is the organism classically found within macrophages. Cryptococcus is a yeast, not a hyphal mold, and can be both intra- and extracellular.

Microscopic identification of Blastomyces relies on seeing a yeast with a thick, doubly refractive wall and a characteristic broad base connecting the mother cell to the daughter bud. Cryptococcus buds via a much narrower neck.
The multiple buds (ship captain's wheel) morphology is pathognomonic for Paracoccidioides, not Blastomyces.
The wide polysaccharide capsule is the defining feature of Cryptococcus neoformans, visualized via India ink; Blastomyces does not possess this capsule but has a thick cell wall.
Blastomyces is dimorphic (mold in soil, yeast in tissue), but Cryptococcus is not thermally dimorphic; it exists primarily as a yeast in both environments/temperatures.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 416 (Book Page): Note that this organism [Blastomyces] forms a broad-based bud, whereas Cryptococcus neoformans is a yeast that forms a narrow-based bud.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: Ringworm of the scalp (tinea capitis) in children often resolves spontaneously at the onset of puberty. Which of the following physiological factors is primarily responsible for this inhibition of dermatophyte growth?
options: Increased recruitment of neutrophils to the hair follicles
Hormone-associated fatty acids in the skin
Thinning of the keratinized layer of the epidermis
Increased production of secretory IgA in the scalp
Shift in skin pH from acidic to highly alkaline
correctOption: Hormone-associated fatty acids in the skin
optionExplanations: Acute suppuration with neutrophils occurs in some fungal infections like sporotrichosis, but it is not the primary reason for the age-related resolution of tinea capitis.
At puberty, hormonal changes lead to the production of sebaceous secretions containing fatty acids that have a natural inhibitory effect on the growth of dermatophytes.
Thinning of the keratin layer would theoretically make the skin more vulnerable to infection, not less; dermatophytes require keratin for growth.
While IgA is a mucosal defense, the specific mechanism for tinea capitis resolution at puberty is linked to chemical changes in skin lipids rather than antibody titers.
Skin is naturally acidic; significant shifts to alkaline pH are not the primary mechanism by which puberty limits ringworm growth.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 400 (Book Page)-414: [Fatty acids in the skin inhibit dermatophyte growth, and hormone-associated skin changes at puberty limit ringworm of the scalp caused by Trichophyton.]

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of Coccidioides, Paracoccidioides, Blastomyces, Candida, Mucor, Aspergillus, and Cryptococcus
statement: A 34-year-old traveler from Latin America presents with chronic ulcerated lesions of the face and mouth. Microscopic examination of the tissue biopsy reveals thick-walled yeast cells with multiple buds, resembling a 'ship captain's wheel'. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
options: Cryptococcus neoformans
Paracoccidioides brasiliensis
Blastomyces dermatitidis
Candida albicans
Coccidioides immitis
correctOption: Paracoccidioides brasiliensis
optionExplanations: Cryptococcus neoformans is a yeast characterized by a single narrow-based bud and a prominent polysaccharide capsule, which is not seen as a 'captain's wheel'.
Paracoccidioides brasiliensis is a dimorphic fungus endemic to Latin America that classically presents with multiple budding yeasts in a 'captain's wheel' configuration.
Blastomyces dermatitidis is characterized by a single broad-based bud, not multiple buds, and is typically found in North America rather than Latin America.
Candida albicans exists primarily as budding yeasts (blastospores) and pseudohyphae in tissue, and it does not form the characteristic multiple budding yeast clusters of Paracoccidioides.
Coccidioides immitis forms spherules containing endospores in tissue, rather than budding yeasts, and is endemic to the Southwestern United States.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 412 (Book Page): [Table 49–1] Paracoccidioides... Yeasts with multiple buds. [Page 417 (Book Page)]: In pus or tissues, yeast cells with multiple buds resembling a ‘ship captain’s wheel’ are seen microscopically.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of Coccidioides, Paracoccidioides, Blastomyces, Candida, Mucor, Aspergillus, and Cryptococcus
statement: Which diagnostic laboratory technique is specifically employed to visualize the large, non-staining polysaccharide capsule of Cryptococcus neoformans in cerebrospinal fluid?
options: India ink preparation
Calcofluor white fluorescent dye
Gram stain
10% Potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation
Methenamine silver stain
correctOption: India ink preparation
optionExplanations: India ink is a negative stain; the ink particles cannot penetrate the thick polysaccharide capsule of Cryptococcus, creating a clear halo around the yeast cell against a dark background.
Calcofluor white binds to chitin in the fungal cell wall and fluoresces under UV light; while it detects fungi, it is not specific for capsule visualization like India ink.
While Candida is Gram-positive, the Gram stain is poor for visualizing the morphological details of the Cryptococcus capsule and often makes cells look like irregular debris.
KOH is used to dissolve human tissue and proteinaceous debris to visualize fungi in skin scrapings or sputum, but it does not highlight the capsule of Cryptococcus.
Methenamine silver is a tissue stain that binds to the fungal cell wall, turning fungi black, but it is not the classic method for bedside CSF capsule visualization.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 401 (Book Page): (2) the wide capsule of Cryptococcus neoformans seen in India ink preparations of spinal fluid.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of Coccidioides, Paracoccidioides, Blastomyces, Candida, Mucor, Aspergillus, and Cryptococcus
coreConcept: Differential Morphology of Blastomyces vs Cryptococcus
statement: A pathologist is comparing two biopsy specimens containing yeast-like organisms. Specimen 1 shows yeasts with a single bud attached by a broad base, while Specimen 2 shows yeasts with a narrow-based bud and a thick capsule. Which pair of organisms is most likely present?
options: Specimen 1: Coccidioides; Specimen 2: Histoplasma
Specimen 1: Aspergillus; Specimen 2: Mucor
Specimen 1: Paracoccidioides; Specimen 2: Candida
Specimen 1: Blastomyces; Specimen 2: Cryptococcus
Specimen 1: Cryptococcus; Specimen 2: Blastomyces
correctOption: Specimen 1: Blastomyces; Specimen 2: Cryptococcus
optionExplanations: Coccidioides forms spherules containing endospores in tissue, not budding yeasts; Histoplasma forms tiny yeasts inside macrophages.
Aspergillus and Mucor are molds that form hyphae in tissue, not yeasts. Aspergillus has septate hyphae, while Mucor has nonseptate hyphae.
Paracoccidioides typically displays multiple buds (captain's wheel), and Candida is characterized by pseudohyphae and germ tubes.
Blastomyces dermatitidis is distinct for its large yeast cells with a single broad-based bud, whereas Cryptococcus neoformans produces narrow-based buds and a prominent capsule.
This option reverses the morphological descriptions provided in the stem; Cryptococcus has a narrow base, and Blastomyces has a broad base.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 416 (Book Page): The yeast is round with a doubly refractive wall and a single broad-based bud (Figures 49–7 and 49–8). Note that this organism forms a broad-based bud, whereas Cryptococcus neoformans is a yeast that forms a narrow-based bud.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: A child presents with a highly inflamed, circular, pruritic lesion on the arm after playing with a new stray kitten. If the causative agent is a dermatophyte from the genus Microsporum, how is this transmission classified compared to other dermatophytes?
options: Respiratory droplet transmission
Geophilic transmission
Fomite-only transmission
Zoophilic transmission
Anthrophilic transmission
correctOption: Zoophilic transmission
optionExplanations: Dermatophytes do not infect via respiratory droplets; they are restricted to superficial keratinized tissues and are transmitted via direct contact or fomites.
Geophilic fungi reside in the soil. While some dermatophytes live in soil, Microsporum infections in children are most famously associated with pets (zoophilic).
While dermatophytes can survive on fomites (brushes, towels), the primary source in this kitten-related scenario is the live animal reservoir.
Zoophilic dermatophytes, like certain Microsporum species, are primarily animal pathogens that can be transmitted to humans through direct contact with infected pets like cats or dogs.
Anthrophilic fungi are spread primarily from person to person. While some Microsporum species are anthrophilic, the scenario specifies animal contact.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 407 (Book Page): Microsporum is also spread from animals such as dogs and cats. This indicates that to prevent reinfection by Microsporum, the animal must also be treated.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: In the context of fungal dimorphism, how does Histoplasma capsulatum regulate its morphological state to survive the transition from the environment to the human host?
options: It forms thick-walled zygospores to resist the high osmotic pressure of the skin
It remains as a mold regardless of temperature to maximize keratin degradation
It transitions from a mold in the soil (25°C) to a yeast form in the body (37°C)
It utilizes anaerobic fermentation to survive within the low-oxygen environment of the soil
It develops into spherules to prevent phagocytosis by alveolar macrophages
correctOption: It transitions from a mold in the soil (25°C) to a yeast form in the body (37°C)
optionExplanations: Zygospores are sexual spores; Histoplasma primarily propagates asexually via conidia and yeasts in clinical infection.
Histoplasma is dimorphic, not monomorphic like dermatophytes; it must change form to adapt to the host environment.
Thermal dimorphism allows Histoplasma to exist as a nutrient-dispersing mold at 25°C and a survival-oriented yeast at 37°C.
Fungi are generally obligate aerobes or facultative anaerobes; they do not use anaerobic states as a primary trigger for dimorphism.
While dimorphism is a survival trait, spherules are specific to Coccidioides; Histoplasma specifically becomes a yeast to survive inside macrophages.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 399 (Book Page): Several medically important fungi are thermally dimorphic (i.e., they form different structures at different temperatures). They exist as molds in the environment at ambient temperature and as yeasts ... in human tissues at body temperature. Page 414 (Book Page): H. capsulatum is a dimorphic fungus that exists as a mold in soil and as a yeast in tissue.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: What is the characteristic tissue morphology of the yeast phase of Sporothrix schenckii seen in clinical specimens?
options: Dematiaceous round fungal cells
Cigar-shaped budding yeasts
Endospores within spherules
Broad-based budding yeasts
Tuberculate macroconidia
correctOption: Cigar-shaped budding yeasts
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Dematiaceous (dark-pigmented) cells are seen in chromomycosis, caused by fungi like Fonsecaea or Phialophora.
Correct. The 'cigar-shaped' yeast is the unique morphological descriptor for Sporothrix in infected tissue.
Incorrect. Spherules containing endospores are found in Coccidioides immitis infections.
Incorrect. Broad-based budding yeasts are the hallmark of Blastomyces dermatitidis.
Incorrect. Tuberculate macroconidia are the asexual spores of Histoplasma capsulatum found in environmental mold cultures, not in human tissue.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 410 (Book Page): In the clinical laboratory, round or cigar-shaped budding yeasts are seen in tissue specimens.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of Coccidioides, Paracoccidioides, Blastomyces, Candida, Mucor, Aspergillus, and Cryptococcus
statement: A pathologist is comparing two tissue biopsies from patients with systemic fungal infections. Biopsy A shows large, thick-walled yeasts with single buds attached by a wide base. Biopsy B shows large, thick-walled yeasts with multiple buds, resembling a 'ship captain's wheel'. What is the most likely identity of these two organisms?
options: A: Candida albicans; B: Cryptococcus neoformans
A: Aspergillus fumigatus; B: Mucor indicus
A: Paracoccidioides brasiliensis; B: Blastomyces dermatitidis
A: Blastomyces dermatitidis; B: Paracoccidioides brasiliensis
A: Coccidioides immitis; B: Histoplasma capsulatum
correctOption: A: Blastomyces dermatitidis; B: Paracoccidioides brasiliensis
optionExplanations: Candida albicans is characterized by pseudohyphae and blastoconidia, while Cryptococcus is characterized by a wide capsule and narrow-based budding, neither of which match the descriptions provided.
Aspergillus and Mucor are both molds that form hyphae in tissue, not the budding yeast forms described in the stem.
This option reverses the correct morphologies; Blastomyces is the broad-based single bud, not the multiple bud.

Blastomyces dermatitidis is classically identified by its broad-based budding yeast morphology in tissue. Paracoccidioides brasiliensis is distinguished by its 'multiple buds' or 'pilot wheel' appearance, where several daughter cells bud from a single mother cell.
Coccidioides forms spherules containing endospores, not budding yeasts, and Histoplasma is seen as small yeasts within macrophages.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 415 (Book Page): [The yeast is round with a doubly refractive wall and a single broad-based bud (Figures 49-7 and 49-8)... Paracoccidioides brasiliensis... multiple buds... resembling a 'ship captain’s wheel' (Figures 49-9 and 49-10).]

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: Regarding the thermal dimorphism of Sporothrix schenckii, which of the following correctly describes its morphological state in the laboratory compared to its state in a patient's wound?
options: Molds with tuberculate macroconidia at 37°C; yeasts in the wound
Spherules at 20°C in the lab; hyphae in the wound
Yeast at 20°C in the lab; mold in the wound
Pseudohyphae at 37°C in the lab; yeasts in the wound
Hyphae with daisy-like conidia at 20°C; yeasts in the wound
correctOption: Hyphae with daisy-like conidia at 20°C; yeasts in the wound
optionExplanations: Tuberculate macroconidia are the hallmark of the mold phase of Histoplasma capsulatum, not Sporothrix.
Spherules are the tissue form of Coccidioides, not Sporothrix.
Dimorphic fungi exist as molds at lower temperatures (environment/lab) and yeasts at higher temperatures (body tissue).
Sporothrix forms true yeasts, not pseudohyphae; pseudohyphae are typical of Candida.
In the environment or lab (20-25°C), Sporothrix grows as a mold with characteristic daisy-like conidia; in human tissue (37°C), it transitions to the yeast phase.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 410 (Book Page): Sporothrix schenckii is a dimorphic fungus. The mold form lives on plants, and the yeast form occurs in human tissue... culture at 20°C shows hyphae with daisy-like conidia.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: Which of the following diagnostic criteria is specifically used to identify tinea capitis caused by Microsporum species by producing a characteristic fluorescence?
options: Detection of IgG antibodies using a complement fixation test
Microscopic visualization of tuberculate macroconidia
Application of ultraviolet light from a Wood’s lamp to the lesion
The presence of arthrospores within a spherule on KOH mount
Formation of germ tubes in serum after incubation at 37°C
correctOption: Application of ultraviolet light from a Wood’s lamp to the lesion
optionExplanations: Serologic tests like complement fixation are used for systemic mycoses (e.g., Coccidioidomycosis), not for superficial dermatophyte infections.
Tuberculate macroconidia are used to identify Histoplasma capsulatum in culture, not dermatophytes.
A Wood's lamp (UV light) causes hairs infected with certain Microsporum species to fluoresce, aiding in the clinical diagnosis of tinea capitis.
Spherules are seen in Coccidioides infections, whereas dermatophytes show septate hyphae on KOH mounts.
Germ tube formation is a diagnostic test for Candida albicans.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 409 (Book Page): Tinea capitis lesions caused by Microsporum species can be detected by seeing fluorescence when the lesions are exposed to ultraviolet light from a Wood’s lamp.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: Regarding the physiological regulation and intracellular cycle of Histoplasma capsulatum, which statement correctly describes its replication and spread within the human host?
options: It replicates as small budding yeasts within macrophages and spreads to the liver and spleen.
It remains as microconidia in the alveoli and induces an immediate IgE-mediated hypersensitivity.
It undergoes asexual budding to form long chains of pseudohyphae that evade neutrophils.
It replicates as spherules that eventually rupture to release endospores into the bloodstream.
It exists as a mold in the lungs where it forms hyphae that invade blood vessel walls.
correctOption: It replicates as small budding yeasts within macrophages and spreads to the liver and spleen.
optionExplanations: Histoplasma capsulatum is an intracellular pathogen; after being engulfed, it replicates as yeasts within the macrophage and uses these cells to travel via the reticuloendothelial system to the liver and spleen.

Microconidia are the infectious form but they must convert to yeasts to replicate. Immediate hypersensitivity is associated with allergies to spores (e.g., Aspergillus), not the primary infection cycle of Histoplasma.
Pseudohyphae are characteristic of Candida species; Histoplasma replicates as discrete oval yeasts.
The spherule-endospore cycle is the lifecycle of Coccidioides, not Histoplasma.

Histoplasma does not exist as a mold in the lungs; it converts to a yeast form upon inhalation and does not primarily cause disease through hyphal vessel invasion (which is seen in Aspergillus or Mucor).
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 415 (Book Page): Inhaled spores are engulfed by macrophages and develop into yeast forms... The organisms spread widely throughout the body, especially to the liver and spleen... H. capsulatum occurs as an oval budding yeast inside macrophages.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of Coccidioides, Paracoccidioides, Blastomyces, Candida, Mucor, Aspergillus, and Cryptococcus
statement: A pathologist is reviewing a biopsy from an ulcerated skin lesion and identifies yeast cells. Which feature most reliably differentiates Blastomyces dermatitidis from Cryptococcus neoformans?
options: The presence of septate hyphae with dichotomous branching
The presence of a thick, India ink-positive polysaccharide capsule
The observation of a single broad-based bud connecting daughter cells
The intracellular location of the yeast within circulating neutrophils
The ability of the organism to form germ tubes at 37°C
correctOption: The observation of a single broad-based bud connecting daughter cells
optionExplanations: Septate hyphae are characteristic of molds like Aspergillus; neither Blastomyces nor Cryptococcus exist as hyphae in human tissue (they are yeasts).
A large polysaccharide capsule is the hallmark of Cryptococcus neoformans and is visualized with India ink, not Blastomyces.
Correct. Blastomyces is distinguished by its single, broad-based bud, while Cryptococcus displays narrow-based budding.
Blastomyces is typically extracellular in tissue; Histoplasma is the fungus primarily characterized by its intracellular location within macrophages.
Germ tube formation is a specific diagnostic test for Candida albicans when incubated in serum for 3 hours at 37°C.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 402 (Book Page): The yeast is round with a doubly refractive wall and a single broad-based bud... Note that this organism forms a broad-based bud, whereas Cryptococcus neoformans is a yeast that forms a narrow-based bud.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: A family presents to the clinic with ringworm infections. The father has tinea pedis, and the young daughter has tinea capitis. The family recently adopted a stray puppy that also has scaly skin patches. To prevent reinfection of the daughter, which genus must be specifically targeted in the treatment of the animal?
options: Trichophyton
Malassezia
Microsporum
Epidermophyton
Histoplasma
correctOption: Microsporum
optionExplanations: Trichophyton is primarily spread from person to person (anthropophilic) and is not the primary genus associated with zoonotic transmission from domestic pets like dogs.
Malassezia is part of the normal human skin flora and causes tinea versicolor; it is not typically acquired as a 'ringworm' infection from a puppy.

Microsporum (specifically M. canis) is a well-known zoophilic dermatophyte. If a domestic animal is infected, it can act as a reservoir, and the animal must be treated to prevent recurrent human infection.
Epidermophyton is also primarily anthropophilic and is not known for causing tinea capitis or being transmitted from dogs.
Histoplasma is a systemic fungus acquired via inhalation of spores from the environment (soil/bird droppings), not through direct contact with a puppy's skin.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 407 (Book Page): Microsporum is also spread from animals such as dogs and cats. This indicates that to prevent reinfection by Microsporum, the animal must also be treated.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of Coccidioides, Paracoccidioides, Blastomyces, Candida, Mucor, Aspergillus, and Cryptococcus
statement: When distinguishing between various yeasts in a clinical specimen, which characteristic best identifies Blastomyces dermatitidis compared to Cryptococcus neoformans?
options: Ability to grow as a mold at 37°C
Presence of a wide polysaccharide capsule
Presence of multiple buds on a single mother cell
Formation of germ tubes in serum
Yeast cells with a single broad-based bud
correctOption: Yeast cells with a single broad-based bud
optionExplanations: Blastomyces is dimorphic, meaning it grows as a mold in the soil (low temperature) and a yeast in the body (37°C), but it does not grow as a mold at body temperature.
A wide polysaccharide capsule is the defining feature of Cryptococcus neoformans and is visualized using India ink, whereas Blastomyces lacks such a capsule.
Multiple buds are characteristic of Paracoccidioides brasiliensis, while Blastomyces typically presents with only a single broad-based bud per yeast cell.
Germ tube formation is a specific diagnostic test for Candida albicans when incubated in serum, not a feature used to identify Blastomyces.
Blastomyces dermatitidis is uniquely characterized in tissue by thick walls and a single bud that attaches to the mother cell via a wide base.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 416 (Book Page): The yeast is round with a doubly refractive wall and a single broad-based bud (Figures 49–7 and 49–8). Note that this organism forms a broad-based bud, whereas Cryptococcus neoformans is a yeast that forms a narrow-based bud.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: Regarding the thermal dimorphism of Sporothrix schenckii, which of the following accurately describes its morphological transition in the laboratory?
options: It grows as a mold with arthrospores at 37°C and as a spherule at 25°C
It grows as a yeast at 20°C and as a mold with daisy-like conidia at 37°C
It exists as a nonseptate mold regardless of temperature in clinical culture
It grows as a yeast with multiple buds at 20°C and as a single-budding yeast at 37°C
It grows as a mold with daisy-like conidia at 20°C and as a budding yeast at 37°C
correctOption: It grows as a mold with daisy-like conidia at 20°C and as a budding yeast at 37°C
optionExplanations: This describes the transition of Coccidioides, except that Coccidioides forms spherules in tissue (37°C), not at 25°C.
The temperatures are reversed; dimorphic fungi exist in the mold form at lower environmental temperatures (20-25°C) and the yeast form at body temperature (37°C).
Sporothrix is dimorphic, not monomorphic. Furthermore, its mold form consists of septate hyphae, not nonseptate hyphae (which are characteristic of Mucor/Rhizopus).

This does not describe Sporothrix; multiple buds are characteristic of Paracoccidioides yeast, and single buds are seen in many yeasts, but the temperature-dependent mold-to-yeast switch is missing here.
Sporothrix is dimorphic; at room temperature (20°C), it grows as a mold (hyphae) with conidia in a daisy-like arrangement, and at body temperature (37°C), it transforms into the yeast phase.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 409 (Book Page): Sporothrix ... KOH prep shows cigar-shaped yeasts culture at 20°C shows hyphae with daisy-like conidia. Page 410 (Book Page): S. schenckii is a dimorphic fungus. The mold form lives on plants, and the yeast form occurs in human tissue.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: A laboratory technician compares two KOH preparations from different skin scrapings. Slide A shows only septate hyphae, while Slide B shows a mixture of both budding yeast cells and hyphae. What is the most likely diagnostic contrast between these two samples?
options: Slide A represents a Dermatophytosis; Slide B represents Malassezia infection
Slide A is an infection of the hair; Slide B is an infection of the nails
Slide A represents Sporotrichosis; Slide B represents Histoplasmosis
Slide A shows an opportunistic mold; Slide B shows a systemic dimorphic fungus
Slide A represents Tinea versicolor; Slide B represents Tinea corporis
correctOption: Slide A represents a Dermatophytosis; Slide B represents Malassezia infection
optionExplanations: Dermatophytes (Slide A) typically appear only as septate hyphae in KOH. Malassezia (Slide B) causes Tinea versicolor and characteristically shows both yeasts and hyphae (often called 'spaghetti and meatballs').
Both hair and nail dermatophytoses would show hyphae (and sometimes spores in hair), but wouldn't explain the yeast/hyphae mixture seen in Malassezia.
Sporothrix appears as cigar-shaped yeasts in tissue, and Histoplasma appears as small yeasts within macrophages. Neither typically presents this way in a standard skin KOH scraping.
While technically true that some molds are septate, the specific combination in Slide B is diagnostic for Malassezia, a cutaneous fungus, not a systemic dimorphic one in this context.
This is reversed. Tinea versicolor (Malassezia) shows both yeasts and hyphae, while Tinea corporis (dermatophytes) shows only hyphae.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 409 (Book Page): Scrapings of skin or nail placed in 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) on a glass slide show septate hyphae under microscopy [for dermatophytes]... Tinea versicolor... The lesions contain both budding yeast cells and hyphae. Diagnosis is usually made by observing this mixture in KOH preparations.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of Coccidioides, Paracoccidioides, Blastomyces, Candida, Mucor, Aspergillus, and Cryptococcus
statement: A medical student is examining a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample from a patient with suspected fungal meningitis. Upon adding India ink to the specimen, the student observes yeasts surrounded by a clear, wide, unstained zone. Which of the following fungal components is primarily responsible for this microscopic appearance?
options: Surface proteins that facilitate adherence to the meningeal lining.
A network of septate hyphae with dichotomous branching.
A polysaccharide capsule composed of glucuronoxylomannan.
A thick cell wall composed of chitin and N-acetylglucosamine.
A cell membrane containing high concentrations of cholesterol.
correctOption: A polysaccharide capsule composed of glucuronoxylomannan.
optionExplanations: While surface proteins are important for pathogenesis and adherence, they do not have the physical volume or refractive properties required to create the halo observed in India ink preparations.
Cryptococcus exists primarily as a yeast in both the environment and tissue; it does not form a network of septate hyphae, which is more characteristic of molds like Aspergillus.

Cryptococcus neoformans is unique among medically important fungi for possessing a thick polysaccharide capsule that repels the carbon particles in India ink, resulting in a visible clear halo or 'wide capsule' against a dark background.
Chitin is the primary structural component of all fungal cell walls, providing rigidity, but it does not produce the characteristic clear halo seen with India ink staining.
Fungal cell membranes contain ergosterol rather than cholesterol, which is the primary sterol found in human cell membranes; this difference is the basis for many antifungal therapies.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 401 (Book Page): [the wide capsule of Cryptococcus neoformans seen in India ink preparations of spinal fluid.]

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of Coccidioides, Paracoccidioides, Blastomyces, Candida, Mucor, Aspergillus, and Cryptococcus
statement: Which diagnostic test is used specifically to visualize the capsule of Cryptococcus neoformans in cerebrospinal fluid samples?
options: Sabouraud’s agar culture
Potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation
Complement fixation test
India ink preparation
Calcofluor white stain
correctOption: India ink preparation
optionExplanations: Sabouraud’s agar is a general fungal culture medium; it allows the organism to grow but is not a direct visualization technique for the capsule.
KOH is used to dissolve human tissue and cellular debris to better visualize various fungal structures, but it does not highlight the capsule of Cryptococcus.
Complement fixation is a serological test used to detect antibodies, not to visualize the physical structure of the organism.
India ink is a negative stain; the ink particles are excluded by the large polysaccharide capsule, creating a clear 'halo' around the yeast cell.
Calcofluor white is a fluorescent dye that binds to cellulose and chitin in fungal cell walls.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 401 (Book Page): (2) the wide capsule of Cryptococcus neoformans seen in India ink preparations of spinal fluid.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: Why does ringworm of the scalp, specifically when caused by certain Trichophyton species, often resolve spontaneously or become much less common after a child reaches puberty?
options: A switch from Th2 to Th1 cellular immune responses due to testosterone/estrogen
Increased temperature of the scalp during puberty which inhibits fungal growth
Hormone-associated skin changes and the inhibitory effect of fatty acids in the skin
Increased production of IgA in the sebaceous glands of the scalp
The thickening of the keratin layer which prevents fungal enzyme penetration
correctOption: Hormone-associated skin changes and the inhibitory effect of fatty acids in the skin
optionExplanations: While sex hormones do influence the immune system, the specific reason cited for the age-related resistance to tinea capitis is the change in skin chemistry and hormones at the local site.
Scalp temperature remains relatively constant and is not high enough to inhibit the growth of these molds; most dermatophytes thrive at body temperature or room temperature regardless of age.
At puberty, sebaceous glands increase the production of sebum, which contains fatty acids. These fatty acids have a natural fungistatic effect against dermatophytes like Trichophyton.
While mucosal IgA is important for other pathogens, the primary mechanism of resistance to tinea capitis at puberty is biochemical and physical, not IgA-mediated.
The thickness of the skin does not significantly change in a way that prevents dermatophyte infection; dermatophytes specifically thrive in keratinized layers.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 400 (Book Page): Fatty acids in the skin inhibit dermatophyte growth, and hormone-associated skin changes at puberty limit ringworm of the scalp caused by Trichophyton.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: In the laboratory diagnosis of systemic mycoses, how does the tissue morphology of Histoplasma capsulatum contrast with that of Blastomyces dermatitidis?
options: Histoplasma is a nonseptate mold, whereas Blastomyces is a septate mold.
Histoplasma cells have a wide polysaccharide capsule, while Blastomyces cells lack a cell wall.
Histoplasma forms spherules, whereas Blastomyces forms cigar-shaped yeasts.

Spherules containing endospores are pathognomonic for Coccidioides immitis and do not occur in either Blastomyces or Cryptococcus.
Nonseptate hyphae are characteristic of the Zygomycetes (Mucor and Rhizopus), which do not typically present as budding yeasts in clinical specimens.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur, Sporothrix schenckii, and Histoplasma capsulatum
statement: When performing a potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation on skin scrapings to differentiate between various superficial fungal infections, which morphological finding specifically distinguishes Malassezia furfur from the dermatophytes?
options: A mixture of budding yeast cells and short hyphae
Spherules containing numerous small endospores
Cigar-shaped budding yeasts within giant cells
Branching nonseptate hyphae with right-angle branching
The presence of septate hyphae without any yeast forms
correctOption: A mixture of budding yeast cells and short hyphae
optionExplanations: Malassezia furfur (causing tinea versicolor) classically shows a 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance, which consists of both short hyphae and budding yeast cells.
Spherules containing endospores are pathognomonic for Coccidioides immitis, a systemic pathogen, and are not found in superficial skin scrapings.
Cigar-shaped yeasts are characteristic of Sporothrix schenckii in tissue, which causes subcutaneous rather than superficial infection.
Nonseptate hyphae with wide branching are characteristic of Mucor or Rhizopus, which are opportunistic molds, not superficial dermatological pathogens.
Septate hyphae without yeast forms are the classic finding for dermatophytes (Trichophyton, etc.), not Malassezia.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 409 (Book Page): The lesions [of tinea versicolor] contain both budding yeast cells and hyphae. Diagnosis is usually made by observing this mixture in KOH preparations of skin scrapings.

statement: A clinical microbiologist is reviewing potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparations of skin scrapings from two different patients. Patient X will show spherules, while Patient Y will show cigar-shaped yeasts

The 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance (yeasts + hyphae) is diagnostic for Malassezia (tinea versicolor), whereas dermatophytes show only septate hyphae.
Spherules are characteristic of Coccidioides, and cigar-shaped yeasts are characteristic of Sporothrix schenckii.

statement: In the microscopic identification of budding yeasts from clinical specimens, how is Blastomyces dermatitidis distinguished from Cryptococcus neoformans?
options: Blastomyces forms a narrow-based bud, while Cryptococcus forms a broad-based bud.
Blastomyces is encapsulated, while Cryptococcus lacks a capsule.
Blastomyces forms a broad-based bud, while Cryptococcus forms a narrow-based bud.
Blastomyces forms multiple buds, while Cryptococcus forms a single bud.
Blastomyces produces pseudohyphae, while Cryptococcus produces true hyphae.
correctOption: Blastomyces forms a broad-based bud, while Cryptococcus forms a narrow-based bud.
optionExplanations: This statement is the exact opposite of the correct diagnostic morphology; Blastomyces is characterized by the 'broad-based' attachment of the daughter cell.
Cryptococcus neoformans is famously encapsulated (visible via India ink), whereas Blastomyces dermatitidis is not known for a thick polysaccharide capsule.

Blastomyces dermatitidis is identified by its large, thick-walled yeast cells with a single bud that is attached by a wide or broad base, whereas Cryptococcus neoformans has a characteristic narrow-based bud and is typically encapsulated.
Paracoccidioides forms multiple buds; both Blastomyces and Cryptococcus typically form a single bud during asexual reproduction.
Neither Blastomyces nor Cryptococcus typically form pseudohyphae or true hyphae in human tissue; both exist primarily as yeasts in the host environment.

The identification of macroconidia with fingerlike projections

The visualization of a mixture of both budding yeast cells and hyphae
The finding of barrel-shaped arthrospores alternating with empty cells
correctOption: The visualization of a mixture of both budding yeast cells and hyphae
optionExplanations: Cigar-shaped yeasts are the tissue form of Sporothrix schenckii, which is a subcutaneous fungus, not a superficial skin scraping finding like Malassezia.
Tuberculate macroconidia with fingerlike projections are characteristic of Histoplasma capsulatum in culture at 25°C, not Malassezia in clinical skin specimens.
Dermatophytes typically show only septate hyphae in KOH preparations. The absence of yeast forms would point away from Malassezia furfur.
Malassezia furfur, the cause of tinea versicolor, is identified by the characteristic 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance—a mixture of short hyphae and budding yeasts.
Arthrospores are characteristic of Coccidioides immitis in culture or soil, not Malassezia or dermatophytes in skin scrapings.
